positions/framework-hypothesis/oneLine: The six days of Genesis 1 are a literary-theological framework — two parallel triads of “kingdoms” (days 1-3) and “rulers” (days 4-6) crowned by the Sabbath — that teach who created and why, not how long or in what sequence.
positions/framework-hypothesis/coreClaim: Genesis 1 is exalted, structured prose with a deliberate pattern.
Days 1-3 form realms; days 4-6 fill them with rulers (light/luminaries; sky and sea/birds and fish; land/animals and humans).
Genesis 2:5 assumes ordinary providence during creation, ruling out a rapid miraculous sequence.
The seventh day has no end, showing the days are not ordinary.
The text addresses ancient Near Eastern idolatry, not modern science.
positions/framework-hypothesis/origin: Proposed by Dutch scholar Arie Noordtzij (1924), developed by N. H. Ridderbos (1957) and Meredith Kline (1958, 1996); later defended by Henri Blocher and Bruce Waltke; related to John Walton’s “cosmic temple” reading (2009).
positions/framework-hypothesis/strongest: It takes the literary craft of Genesis seriously and stands in continuity with Augustine’s non-chronological reading.
It frees exegesis from concordist pressure in either direction.
It explains anomalies such as light before the sun.
Young-earth creationists object that “evening and morning” and Exodus 20:11 imply real days and that the framework reading seems tailored to accommodate science.
Some Reformed critics argue the Westminster Confession’s “in the space of six days” excludes it (debated in the PCA and OPC, 1990s-2000s).
Others question whether the two-triad scheme fits all the details.
positions/framework-hypothesis/responses: Framework advocates answer that Exodus 20:11 is analogical (God’s “week” as pattern for ours), as is God’s “rest” and “refreshment” (31:17).
They note that Noordtzij proposed the view before modern creation-evolution debates heated up and argue from the text, not science.
positions/framework-hypothesis/consequen: Allowed many confessional Reformed churches to remain agnostic on the age of the earth.
Debated in Presbyterian Church in America study committee (2000), which judged several views acceptable.
positions/evolutionary-creation/oneLine: God is the Creator of all things, and the evolution of life over billions of years through common descent is the means by which he has providentially brought about living things, including the human body.
positions/evolutionary-creation/coreClai: Mainstream science (old universe, common descent) is accurate about how life developed.
Natural processes are God’s ongoing work, not rivals to him (secondary causes).
Genesis teaches theology — God, humanity’s vocation, sin — in ancient literary forms, not modern science.
Humans uniquely bear God’s image; views of Adam range from a historical pair/representatives to an archetype.
positions/evolutionary-creation/origin: Accepted by 19th-century Christians such as Asa Gray, Charles Kingsley, Aubrey Moore (Lux Mundi, 1889), James Orr and B. B. Warfield; opened in Catholic teaching by Humani Generis (1950) and John Paul II (1996); advocated today by BioLogos (2007), Faraday Institute and many Orthodox and mainline theologians.
positions/evolutionary-creation/stronges: It allows full intellectual honesty about the overwhelming convergent evidence (fossils, genetics, biogeography).
It sees God’s creativity in a world that makes itself under his providence, in line with Aquinas’ secondary causation.
It removes needless obstacles to faith for scientifically trained people.
It reads Genesis within its ancient Near Eastern context.
Young-earth creationists argue it undermines the historicity of Adam, the fall and the link between sin and death, and so the gospel (Romans 5; 1 Corinthians 15).
Intelligent-design proponents argue that unguided mechanisms cannot generate biological information and that “theistic evolution” concedes too much to naturalism.
Critics ask how a good God could use a process involving vast suffering, predation and extinction over millions of years.
positions/evolutionary-creation/response: Evolutionary creationists answer that many hold to a historical Adam (as representative or within a population) and that Paul’s theology rests on universal sin and grace, not on a particular biology.
They respond that evolution is not “unguided” in a theological sense: God sustains and directs all natural processes.
On suffering they develop “only way” or cruciform theodicies (creation as costly and free), acknowledging difficulty.
positions/evolutionary-creation/conseque: Became the default view in Catholic, Orthodox and mainline Protestant scholarship and a growing evangelical minority.
Generated new work on human origins, original sin and animal suffering.
positions/intelligent-design/oneLine: Certain features of the universe and of living things are best explained by an intelligent cause rather than undirected processes, and this inference can be made by scientific methods.
positions/intelligent-design/coreClaims/: Specified complexity and irreducible complexity are reliable markers of design.
Undirected natural selection cannot account for the origin of life’s information or certain molecular machines.
ID does not, as such, identify the designer or require a young earth.
positions/intelligent-design/origin: Grew out of 1980s critiques of origin-of-life research; launched by Phillip E. Johnson’s Darwin on Trial (1991), Michael Behe’s Darwin’s Black Box (1996) and William Dembski’s The Design Inference (1998); organised through the Discovery Institute (1996).
positions/intelligent-design/strongestAr: It challenges methodological naturalism’s monopoly in science and asks a legitimate question about the origin of biological information.
Its arguments resemble everyday design inferences (archaeology, forensics, SETI).
It unites old-earth, young-earth and some theistic-evolution believers and non-Christians in questioning neo-Darwinism.
positions/intelligent-design/strongestOb: Most biologists, including many Christians, argue that proposed examples of irreducible complexity have plausible evolutionary pathways (e.g. co-option of parts of the flagellum).
Evolutionary creationists and Thomists argue ID makes God a “god of the gaps” competing with natural causes rather than the Creator of all causes.
The Kitzmiller court (2005) found that ID functions as a re-labelled creationism and is not science.
positions/intelligent-design/responses/0: ID proponents answer that design is inferred from positive evidence (information), not mere gaps.
positions/intelligent-design/responses/1: They contend that the Kitzmiller judge overreached and that mainstream science has failed to give detailed Darwinian pathways.
positions/intelligent-design/consequence: Revived interest in classical design arguments and in cosmic fine-tuning.
positions/thomist-concurrence/oneLine: God, the transcendent first cause, gives being and activity to every creature at every moment, while creatures are genuine secondary causes acting according to their natures — including free creatures acting freely.
positions/thomist-concurrence/coreClaims: God conserves all things in being continually.
God concurs with every action of creatures, as first cause, without competing with them on the same level.
Creatures, including free agents and chance processes, are real causes.
God’s providence orders all things to their ends, permitting evil for greater goods.
positions/thomist-concurrence/origin: Rooted in Augustine and Boethius; systematised by Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I q.22, q.103-105; Summa contra Gentiles III); refined by Domingo Báñez (physical premotion) and in debates with Molinism.
positions/thomist-concurrence/strongestA: It preserves both divine sovereignty and real creaturely causation, avoiding occasionalism and deism.
Because God is not one cause among others, divine and creaturely agency are not in zero-sum competition.
It provides a framework in which natural science (studying secondary causes) and theology need not conflict.
positions/thomist-concurrence/strongestO: Molinists object that Thomist premotion makes God the determining cause of sinful acts, threatening freedom.
Open and process theists argue that concurrence leaves no room for real creaturely contribution or for God being affected.
Some analytic philosophers find the “non-competitive” claim obscure or incoherent.
positions/thomist-concurrence/responses/: Thomists answer that God causes the being of the act but not its defect: sin is a privation for which the creature is responsible.
They maintain that transcendent causation is analogical and cannot be modelled as a stronger version of creaturely causation.
positions/thomist-concurrence/consequenc: Became the mainstream Catholic account and influenced Reformed scholastics.
Underlies many contemporary evolutionary-creation accounts of divine action.
positions/calvinist-meticulous-providenc: Meticulous providence (Reformed)

Calvinist providence
compatibilist providence
God not only sustains the world but governs every event, including free choices and evils, according to his eternal decree, for his glory and the good of his people — without being the author of sin.
Nothing happens by chance or bare permission; God’s will is the ultimate cause of all that happens.
God ordains evil events while remaining holy; humans remain responsible (compatibilism).
Providence is a comfort: all things work together for good to those who love God.
God works ordinarily through means but is free to work without, above and against them.

It takes at face value the many texts where God ordains even evil acts for good (Joseph, the cross).
It gives believers deep assurance: nothing escapes God’s purpose.
It coheres with God’s omniscience and the doctrine of unconditional election.
Arminians and open theists object that it makes God the author of sin and empties human freedom and responsibility.
Many find it pastorally harmful in face of atrocity: did God “ordain” the Holocaust?
Thomists and Orthodox note a danger of reducing divine causality to a univocal “super-cause” determining creatures.
Reformed theologians answer with compatibilism: humans act freely when they do what they want, and God ordains through secondary causes without coercion (Westminster 3.1; 5.2).
They distinguish God’s decretive and preceptive will and insist that the cross shows God bringing the greatest good from the greatest evil.
Shaped Puritan and Reformed piety (providence journals, fast days).
Central in modern Calvinist revival and in debates with open theism.
positions/irenaean-soul-making/oneLine: God created humanity immature and placed it in a challenging world so that through free struggle, suffering and growth it might mature into the likeness of God; evil is permitted as the necessary environment for soul-making.
positions/irenaean-soul-making/coreClaim: Humanity was created in the image of God but has yet to grow into the likeness.
A world without pain and risk could not produce virtues such as courage, compassion and faith.
God keeps an “epistemic distance” so that faith and love are free.
The process will be completed beyond this life (Hick held a universalist outcome).
positions/irenaean-soul-making/origin: Inspired by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.37-39, c.180), echoed by Schleiermacher; named and systematised by John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966). Hick borrowed “vale of soul-making” from John Keats.
positions/irenaean-soul-making/proponent: Many Eastern Orthodox emphases on growth toward theosis
positions/irenaean-soul-making/strongest: It fits a world of long evolutionary development better than a paradise-and-fall narrative.
It gives meaning to suffering as formative rather than merely punitive.
It resonates with Eastern Christian emphasis on growth toward theosis.
Critics (e.g. D. Z. Phillips, John K. Roth) argue that horrendous evils such as the Holocaust destroy rather than make souls and that treating them as instruments is morally obscene.
Augustinians object that it underplays the fall and makes evil a divine necessity.
The amount and distribution of suffering (children, animals) seems far beyond what soul-making needs.
positions/irenaean-soul-making/responses: Hick answered that soul-making requires a world of real, not token, danger, and that eschatological fulfilment ultimately justifies the process.
Defenders argue that the theodicy concerns the general conditions of the world, not a justification of every particular evil.
positions/irenaean-soul-making/consequen: Popular in 20th-century philosophy of religion and in evolutionary theodicies.
Prompted renewed study of Irenaeus’ theology of growth.
